item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers dynasty is over, or has at least hit a major bump in the road. Thursday's Game 4 loss to the Milwaukee Brewers completed the four-game sweep and sent the two-time defending World Series champions home for the winter. Los Angeles' season is over, as is its stretch of eight consecutive postseason series wins dating back to 2024.
There is no getting around it: The Dodgers looked old in the NLCS. They are old too. Weighed by playing time, they had baseball's oldest collection of position players this season. Will Smith is 31. Shohei Ohtani is 32. Mookie Betts and Teoscar Hernández are 34. Freddie Freeman is 37. The team's core hitters are getting long in the tooth. It was obvious in the NLCS.
That said, the Dodgers remain extremely talented and have the resources (money and tradeable prospects) to improve their roster in the offseason, and again contend in 2027. As bad as they looked in the NLCS, there is no reason to think the Dodgers won't be among baseball's best teams next year -- and on the short list of legitimate World Series contenders.
Here now are three questions facing the Dodgers following their unceremonious NLCS sweep.
1. What is Shohei Ohtani's future?
The two-way star was hindered by health for a large chunk of 2026
In fact, let's talk about his future both short- and long-term. Ohtani was clearly diminished late in the regular season and into the postseason. He played through knee and biceps injuries and simply did not look like himself at the plate. His swing was all arms and there was little hard contact. Before his second-inning home run in Game 4 on Thursday, Ohtani hadn't gone deep since Aug. 18. His power vanished.
Here is Ohtani's expected slugging percentage, which is based on contact quality (exit velocity, launch angle, etc.), throughout this season. It slipped significantly late in the year:
Ohtani did not pitch after July 3 and had a start-and-stop in late August. He rehabbed his injuries, threw bullpen sessions and live batting practice, then had to shut it down before getting back on a mound in a game. Ohtani was playing like his usual MVP self until his injuries popped up in the second half. Once that happened, his season began to circle the drain.
The Dodgers now face two questions with Ohtani. One, does he need offseason surgery on the knee and/or biceps? And if he does need surgery, will the recovery cut into his 2027? Keep in mind that it is a near certainty there will be a lockout this offseason once the CBA expires on Dec. 1, and teams will be banned from communicating with their players. Ohtani would have to rehab on his own, without the team's input.
"It's hard to tell" if he'll require surgery, Ohtani said through an interpreter after Thursday's loss. He does, however, plan to pitch next season, he said.
Offseason surgery is the short-term question. Long-term, regardless of what he said in the shadow of the NLCS sweep, are Ohtani's days as a pitcher numbered? This has been a question since Day 1 of Ohtani's MLB career. His ability to be and remain a two-way player has long been doubted, but he has kept doing it, even if there have been some speed bumps along the way. Ohtani has made a career of doing what people said he couldn't.
The man is 32 now, though. He'll turn 33 next summer and the physical ailments (the knee, the biceps, two UCL surgeries, etc.) are beginning to add up. At some point, Ohtani won't be able to continue as a two-way player, and with each passing season, that point draws closer. Are we there now? Is this it? Is this the end of Ohtani's time as a pitcher? It could be, sure.
My guess is that Ohtani will continue to pitch next season and the Dodgers will happily let him because there is so much value to be gained even if he throws only 75 innings a year. You can't be as good as Ohtani without being stubborn. He's been stubborn in that he insists on playing both ways, and he has continued to do it well. I don't see him dropping it this winter.
It should surprise no one if Ohtani comes out next year, hits 40 home runs, makes 15 ace-caliber starts and wins his fifth MVP unanimously. Do not forget that he was playing at that level as recently as July. The recovery times for the knee and biceps injuries are an offseason question, for sure, and the bottom line is the "will he continue to pitch?" questions will always exist.
2. Will they move on from some longtime stalwarts?
Could the Dodgers say goodbye to Teoscar Hernández or some other familiar names?
The Dodgers are locked into so much of their core: Betts, Freeman, Ohtani, Smith, Kyle Tucker, etc. They aren't going anywhere. That said, there are a few members of the supporting cast, players who have been around for all three recent World Series wins, who might have to be shown the door this offseason for the sake of diversifying the lineup and getting younger and more athletic.
Finding a taker for the final season of Teoscar Hernández's contract and then plugging the precocious Josue De Paula into left field next season is a worthwhile move. It's difficult because Hernández is popular in the clubhouse, but, on the field, De Paula figures to give the Dodgers a better chance to win ballgames moving forward. (De Paula is a poor defender, but so is Hernández.)
The Enrique Hernández era has run its course. He hasn't been even an average regular-season player since 2022, and, for all his postseason heroics, he's barely scraping a .600 OPS in the last two Octobers. Tommy Edman is a better version of the same player. There's no need to carry both on the roster, plus Edman's injuries suggest a smaller role is needed. Less could be more.
Max Muncy stayed healthy this season, hit 29 homers and posted 4.1 WAR, and is owed an affordable $10 million in 2027. Plus, it's a bad offseason to need an infielder. The free-agent market is very thin and you're not likely to find better than Muncy on the trade market. Still, he is 36. Keeping Muncy is justifiable, but it also makes sense to explore alternatives. It never hurts to look.
Blake Treinen has not been healthy and effective at the same time in two years. Alex Vesia's fastball sat 91-92 mph over these last few weeks. Both are free agents and the Dodgers have so many young hard-throwers in Triple-A that I think it's worth turning the page and injecting some younger arms into the bullpen. Evan Phillips may be in this camp, too.
Then again, who am I to doubt the Dodgers and their process? Disappointing NLCS aside, they have been baseball's most successful team of the 2020s, and if they want to remain in the Hernández and Muncy and Treinen business, I won't say they're wrong. It does appear that things are getting a bit stale, though. Incorporating youth would be sensible, and it isn't difficult to find ways to do it.
3. Will they retain Tarik Skubal?
It will cost a lot to keep the trade deadline addition atop the rotation
There's no sense in asking if the Dodgers can retain Tarik Skubal. Of course they can. They are baseball's biggest spenders and he is a Scott Boras client. Typically, all you need to do to get a Boras client is make the biggest offer, which the Dodgers can do. Maybe there's a salary cap that changes the equation. Based on what we know right now, yes, the Dodgers can, of course, re-sign Skubal.
Will they is a different matter. Tyler Glasnow, Blake Snell, and Yoshinobu Yamamoto will return next season. Ohtani could be back on the mound as well, as he indicated is the plan. Emmet Sheehan and Justin Wrobleski both pitched well for long stretches this year and are among the very best No. 5 starter options in the game. Gavin Stone, the team's 2024 innings leader, should return from shoulder surgery as well.
There is never a bad time to sign a pitcher like Skubal, and the Dodgers, with their World Series window still open, are well-positioned to bring him back. They have the money, they can easily clear rotation space, and all indications are that Skubal enjoyed his time with the team after coming over the trade deadline. This feels like a match made in free-agent heaven.
Now it's just a matter of whether the Dodgers can get it done. Perhaps a salary cap or increased competitive balance tax penalties limit their spending; maybe they opt to spread their money around to multiple players; maybe another team just won't be denied. The Dodgers don't absolutely need Skubal. Re-signing him would up their odds of returning to the World Series, though, and help ensure their dynasty didn't end on Thursday night.
For his part, Skubal declined to comment on his impending decision after Game 4.
"I'm not going to comment on my future really at all," Skubal said, via MLB.com. "Today sucks, you know, and that's kind of where my head's at."

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Eric Lauer and other recent Dodgers regular-season helpers
item.dc:creator: Estevão Maximo
item.description: The success of a dominant team over a lengthy period like the Dodgers' relies on an adaptability to work your way through multiple iterations of a roster. While in the postseason you can find success in different ways, one aspect of regular-season success is how you handle injuries, particularly for a team as cautious as the Dodgers. item.content:encoded:
The success of a dominant team over a lengthy period like the Dodgers' relies on an adaptability to work your way through multiple iterations of a roster. While in the postseason you can find success in different ways, one aspect of regular-season success is how you handle injuries, particularly for a team as cautious as the Dodgers.
A common theme in recent seasons has been the Dodgers' pitching staff overcoming all sorts of obstacles to consistently provide terrific numbers. Postseason baseball funnels everything, and meritocracy only takes you so far when the goal is to win short series, but that doesn't mean the impact of productive but unceremoniously overlooked starters shouldn't get the credit it rightfully deserves.
There are layers of this tier, and we're not here to discuss the Justin Wrobleskis of the world, who'll morph into a different but still impactful role because their talent level demands a presence on the postseason roster, one way or another. This is an article for the Eric Lauers — pitchers who served a very specific and much-needed purpose in the regular season, but whose eventual playoff showing would only come in garbage-time scenarios; in Lauer's case, not even that, given he has ended the season on the injured list.
When Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow went down this year, as they often do in the regular season, the Dodgers took to the market early in the season for a veteran steady presence. Lauer did more than just go out there with league-average production or so.
The former Brewer worked on some adjustments with the Dodgers' pitching staff and led the team to a win in each of his first nine starts, boasting an ERA under 3.00 through that period. It'd be no stretch to argue that, at the very least, this chase for a playoff bye would look a lot different with a ton more pressure had it not been for Lauer's timely production. His final line with the Dodgers looks far worse than he pitched due to a couple of blowups against NL Central teams (4.50 ERA in 12 games), but his impact through most of that period was undeniable.
Even in the best of moments for Lauer with the Dodgers prior to his season-ending injury, it was evident that he would not play a key role in the playoffs, but it was about doing a specific job. While he was the best example in this year's current squad, going back through the recent track record, the names pile up, and here we'll look at a few others that might stand out—who perhaps didn't receive the right amount of due at the time, and certainly not when playoff ball rolled around.
Prospects with potentially limited big-league upside
This season's starting pitching problems are a cakewalk in comparison with what this team had to deal with a year ago. On the lookout for starting pitching contributions for much of the 2025 campaign, the Dodgers saw Dustin May come full circle on a sped-up version of your traditional career, entering the innings-eater portion far earlier than anyone would've anticipated, one of three starters on the team to cover 100-plus innings, this despite getting dealt at the deadline.
May, more than probably any other pitcher on this list, really pushed the envelope of what we can consider helpful volume, even with the caveat of potential uncertainty on door number two. It's easy to be dismissive of his ERA in the high 4.00s that got progressively worse until the team dealt him when it got healthier in the second half—through the majority of those innings, though, it literally had no one else. And if we want to get a little cute about it, the health he displayed in that period certainly played a role in helping the Dodgers land the offer they sought, with James Tibbs III joining the fold. It's about finding advantages anywhere.
If May represents the low end of the expectation pool for a pitcher of his caliber receiving this type of role in a contending team, a year prior Gavin Stone showed the best-case scenario. On the way to their second World Series of this era, it was the youngster Stone who led the Dodgers in innings pitched that regular season, before injuries cut short his campaign and development, which has been affected until the present day.
Even before the injuries, it was becoming increasingly clear in the second half of that 2024 campaign that Stone's postseason role would diminish, particularly so after the Dodgers acquired Jack Flaherty at the deadline. The changeup-heavy approach with below-average strikeout numbers caused enough concern that he likely wouldn't have stuck in the rotation one way or another.
Both in very different places right now, one still in the organization, May and Stone were once regarded as highly touted pitching prospects. Although their development wasn't as smooth as the Dodgers would've liked, they showed up to provide support at times of need, and their contributions meant a lot in championship-winning seasons.
Former stars in unique spots
Clayton Kershaw gave his best years to the Dodgers when they weren't nearly at their best and did so with the utmost grace and power. After a second chapter of his career, still dominant but maybe not quite Kershaw-dominant, came to an end in 2023, he stuck around for a couple of more years and only then genuinely looked mortal, but still quite helpful.
Missing the bulk of the 2024 season recovering from shoulder surgery, Kershaw came back healthier for one final year in 2025, and while his All-Star nomination might've been a tad sentimental, the 11-2 record was eye-catching, with a productive 124 ERA+.
Sitting below 90 MPH on his heater, there were clear limitations to what Kershaw could provide, but not only did he appear on the postseason roster. But he also managed to get one immense out in the never-ending Game 3 of that year's World Series. The plan was never to have him play a big role in October, but circumstances gave him a memorable cameo.
Going back to the regular season contributions, Kershaw, alongside May, was one of three Dodgers starters to surpass 100 innings in 2025. On the subject of his impact on that 93-69 record, there was nothing sentimental about it; he thoroughly helped a team that relied on him far more than expected.
Going back a few more years, the Dodgers needed to take on the David Price contract in order for the Mookie Betts deal to go through with Boston. And although that was a bad deal, it didn't mean Price couldn't be of assistance.
Opting out of the 2020 campaign, Price came in 2021 ready to embrace whatever role the Dodgers had for him, and he delivered a 105 ERA+ in over 70 innings, moving back and forth between the rotation and the bullpen. While the rotation was healthier that year, it didn't mean his presence went unnoticed, one of the more heavily used arms navigating between the rotation and the bullpen.
The OGs of this role in this run
When you first started reading this article, there is a decent chance one of the first names that came to mind was Mitch White or, particularly, Ross Stripling — the latter personally thanked by Dave Roberts in the World Series-winning speech back in 2020, a year in which he was traded from the team that August.
Between 2016 and 2019, Stripling pitched nearly 400 innings of regular-season baseball with a 115 ERA+, moving around to whatever role fit the team best. Seeing them finally break through to win it all the year in which he was dealt (2020) quickly made Dave and many others remember all he had done for this team.
It's a shame that at his best in 2018, working primarily as a starter, Stripling saw his campaign cut short due to injury and couldn't be available in that postseason. In 2020, the Dodgers stuck with him as much as possible, but eventually cutting ties seemed like the only answer with an ERA well above 5.00 in a shortened campaign.
White is the ideal example to note how, in most of these cases, whether the Dodgers get these players late, early, or even develop them from the minors, they seem to shine brightest here. In three seasons with the Dodgers, White had a 116 ERA+ in a little over 100 innings. Not only did he fail to reach similar heights after leaving the team, but his exposure was very limited, covering just 79.1 innings in two seasons since. Out of the bigs since 2024.
Surely there were other names in recent memory that we might've skipped over. Let us know who your favorite regular-season starting pitcher contributor is, or even all-time. It's always a fun conversation to have with no right or wrong answer.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Dodgers Temper Stone, Miller Expectations
item.dc:creator: Los Royers
item.description: ATLANTA, GA — Gavin Stone and Bobby Miller delivered encouraging performances during their rehabilitation assignments this week, but Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts tempered expectations that either right-hander is close to claiming a significant role in the major-league pitching staff. item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA, GA — Gavin Stone and Bobby Miller delivered encouraging performances during their rehabilitation assignments this week, but Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts tempered expectations that either right-hander is close to claiming a significant role in the major-league pitching staff.
Stone threw four scoreless innings for Triple-A Oklahoma City, allowing one hit and striking out five. Miller followed with three scoreless innings, one hit allowed and five strikeouts. Their performances naturally raised questions about whether the Dodgers could use either pitcher during the final month of the regular season.
Roberts said both pitchers are progressing, but described their immediate value to the organization in one word.
“Right now, to be quite honest, I think it’s depth,” Roberts said.
Dodgers Temper Expectations for Stone and Miller
The Dodgers entered the season hoping Stone and Miller could eventually strengthen their pitching options, but injuries have prevented both from building a normal workload.
Stone has spent the entire season on the injured list with right shoulder inflammation after missing all of 2025 while recovering from shoulder surgery. He began his rehab assignment with Oklahoma City on August 6 and made his fourth appearance Wednesday.
The right-hander threw 58 pitches, including 41 strikes, and retired the final 10 batters he faced. It was his strongest performance since beginning the assignment and represented another positive step in a comeback that has required considerable patience.
Miller has been on the 60-day injured list all season because of right shoulder soreness. He began his Oklahoma City rehab assignment on August 5 and threw 49 pitches, including 33 strikes, during his three-inning outing Wednesday.
“They’re both doing well. They’re both coming back,” Roberts said. “But I think right now, to be quite honest, I think it’s depth.”
Health and Workload Remain the Priority
Roberts explained that both pitchers have experienced abbreviated seasons without enough competitive innings to immediately be considered finished products.
“Both those guys have had a very abbreviated season, not a lot of competitive baseball,” Roberts said. “And where we’re at on the calendar, I think it’s just getting these guys back to healthy and taking down starts or outings and sustaining that, which they both haven’t done in quite some time.”
That does not eliminate the possibility that Stone or Miller could contribute if the Dodgers need another arm. It does show that the organization is prioritizing their long-term recovery over forcing either pitcher into an immediate role because of one strong outing.
The Dodgers currently have a crowded rotation that includes Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow and Roki Sasaki. Shohei Ohtani is also nearing a return to game action, while Eric Lauer is available to provide length from the bullpen.
That depth gives Los Angeles the flexibility to let Stone and Miller continue rebuilding without rushing them. Roberts had previously discussed Stone as a possible multi-inning bullpen option down the stretch, but his latest comments indicate Stone must first prove he can sustain his workload.
Strong Rehab Outings Still Matter
Roberts’ caution should not erase the progress both pitchers have made. Stone and Miller returned to game action earlier this month after extended absences, giving the Dodgers two additional options who were unavailable for most of the season.
Their long-awaited returns to competitive pitching were important steps by themselves. Their latest results offer more evidence that the rehabilitation process is moving in the right direction.
For now, however, the Dodgers are viewing both starters as insurance rather than building their stretch-run plans around them. Stone and Miller must continue taking down innings, recovering well between appearances and showing that their shoulders can handle a consistent schedule.
If they accomplish that, the Dodgers could revisit their roles. Until then, their strongest contribution may be providing organizational depth while positioning themselves to enter next season healthy.

item.content:encoded:
This is your one-stop shop for every Dodgers stint on the injured list during the 2026 season. We’ll also include every time a player misses time on the paternity list, bereavement leave, or is on the family medical emergency list as well.
Basically any time a player misses time that requires a roster move, we’ll note it here.
During the 2025 season, 28 different Dodgers players spent time on the injured list, some of them for multiple stints. That matched the team total from 2024, while in 2023 the Dodgers saw 34 players miss time on the IL.
Every injured-list stint is a transaction and will also be chronicled on our 40-man roster page. Both are essentially living documents that will be constantly updated throughout the season as these moves happen.
Injured-list stints for pitchers are a minimum of 15 days, and for position players it’s at least 10 days.
During spring training, the Dodgers placed both Evan Phillips and Kiké Hernández on the 60-day injured list, which opened up space on the 40-man roster for other moves. On opening day, six more Dodgers were placed on the injured list, including Blake Snell and Tommy Edman.
For more information on each specific injured list stint, click on the links on the dates in the list below this table.
Note: if you are on a mobile device, these tables will show up best in landscape mode.

item.content:encoded:
Earlier this week after Monday’s 4-1 road victory against the Cincinnati Reds, the Los Angeles Dodgers clinched a playoff berth for the fourteenth consecutive season, an all-time record that ties them with the Atlanta Braves who accomplished it from 1991 to 2005.
A large part of the Dodgers’s success this season has been how good their starting rotation has been. The team has an enormous amount of pitching depth which means they are constantly sending elite starting pitchers to the bump day-in-and-out.
| ERA | WHIP | BB/9 | K/9 |
| 3.45 (2nd) | 1.09 (2nd) | 2.57 (3rd) | 9.19 (4th) |
When I said that the Dodgers have an enormous amount of starting pitching depth, I really did mean a ton of depth.
Their active starting rotation currently consists of Tyler Glasnow, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell and Yoshinobu Yamamoto, but they also have Justin Wrobleski down in the bullpen who put up an excellent first-half in the starting rotation.
You’d think that’s a pretty good rotation by itself and it certainly is, but they have plenty more quality arms remain either in the minors or on the injured list. These names include: Kris Bubic, Landon Knack, Eric Lauer, Roki Sasaki, Emmet Shehaan, Gavin Stone and of course, Shohei Ohtani.
That right there is enough talent to construct two top-10 starting rotations in the majors, which is incredible. The Dodgers’ plethora of depth is great, but it brings us to an interesting discussion.
The Dodgers coaching staff will have a large selection of elite arms to choose from to open up Postseason action, but who is the most logical and realistic starting pitcher for Game 1?
All stats updated prior to games on Thursday, September 17
Blake Snell, LHP
Snell has pitched really well since returning to the starting rotation in early August. Injuries have kept him out most of the season, as his last start prior to his activation in August came back on May 9 — his season was delayed due to left shoulder fatigue. He left his start on Wednesday after just 19 pitches thanks to a groin injury, so his status is currently up in the air.
Snell has made eight total starts this season, six of those coming after he got activated off the injured list again in August. His injuries don’t seem to be lingering as he’s proven to still be one of the best pitchers in the majors.
Across 38.2 innings pitched, Snell owns a 1.86 ERA and 1.09 WHIP while his underlying metrics prove that he’s still the elite pitcher we’ve been used to. His expected numbers look great, supported by an excellent 2.16 xERA and 2.94 xFIP proving that he is more than ready for playoff action.
Snell, a veteran of 11 seasons, has plenty of postseason innings under his belt and has proved at times to be really good when it matters the most.
When I say at times, it is because last season across 13 postseason innings, he struggled with a 6.92 ERA and 1.77 WHIP. On the other hand, he’s accumulated 82.2 total playoff innings in his career, pitching to a respectable 3.27 ERA and 1.15 WHIP between the three teams he’s suited up for.
Keep in mind that Dave Roberts elected to start Snell in Game 1 of the National League Wild Card last year against the Cincinnati Reds, tossing seven quality innings allowing just two runs while striking out seven. Maybe they will go the same direction this year.
Tarik Skubal, LHP
This year’s mid-summer trade deadline was headlined by the fact that Detroit Tigers sensation Tarik Skubal would probably be on the move when it was all said and done. Well, it happened and Skubal found himself as the blockbuster of the deadline, being traded to the Dodgers.
Being named the American League Cy Young in back-to-back seasons with the Tigers in both 2024 and 2025, the Dodgers got one of the best starting pitchers in the majors.
The Dodgers likely would’ve been completely fine without him, but when a team has trade assets like the Dodgers do, it was a no-brainer for them to get a deal done.
Skubal was a solid pitcher from 2020 to 2023, but the last three seasons for him, including this year, have been absolutely phenomenal. Presently in 2026, splitting time between the Tigers and Dodgers, Skubal has logged 146.2 innings spanning 24 starts, while pitching to a 2.70 ERA and 0.95 WHIP.
If the Dodgers decide they want their ace to start Game 1, it’s going to be Skubal. He’s proved way more than he needs to show that he can be a reliable option in the Postseason. On top of his regular season success, Skubal has looked almost better in October.
He totaled 39.2 innings between the 2024 and 2025 postseasons with the Tigers and looked utterly dominant, hence his 2.04 ERA and 0.73 WHIP. Skubal’s 2025 epic performance alone is incredible.
Last year in his American League Wild Card start against the Cleveland Guardians, Skubal tossed 7.2 innings, only allowing one earned run off of three hits, along with a whopping 14 strikeouts.
Subsequently in the Tigers American League Divisional Series against the Seattle Mariners, he made two starts, totaling 13 innings where he allowed only three earned runs, seven total hits, while striking out 22 and issuing just one walk — ace quality numbers for sure.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto, RHP
Finally, we have Yamamoto, who might not be getting enough praise that he deserves. He’s in the middle of his third season with the Dodgers and has quietly asserted himself as one of the better starting pitchers in baseball.
The now two-time All-Star finished third in National League Cy Young voting in 2025, and has been incredible thus far in his young career. He’s posted a career ERA of 2.60 so far to go along with a 0.87 WHIP.
This year has been Yamamoto’s best season, and he’s been building off of his 2025 success. Over 27 starts totalling a season-high 179 innings pitched, he’s posted a 2.51 ERA and career-best 0.87 WHIP.
Yamamoto is no stranger to pitching when the lights are the brightest, as he played a massive role contributing to the Dodgers’ World Series title in 2025 against the Toronto Blue Jays. He logged 56 innings of postseason work between 2024 and 2025, resulting in a 2.25 ERA and 0.84 WHIP.
His World Series performance last year was one to remember, tossing 17.2 innings between two starts and a relief appearance with a 1.02 ERA and 0.68 WHIP. In Game 7, he pitched out of relief and closed out the game and series when he got Alejandro Kirk to ground into a double-play.
He’s been an absolute work-horse and should play a huge role this year for the Dodgers in the Postseason, no-matter what role he is given.
The Verdict…
Now onto the final verdict in pinning one of the arms mentioned above to start Game 1 in the playoffs for the Dodgers — a decision that Dave Roberts and his coaching staff won’t take lightly.
The best way to build the Dodgers starting rotation is to alter the handedness each game, so that it’s tougher on whoever their opponent may be. That means with Snell and Skubal both being left-handers and Yamamoto being a right-hander, Yamamoto is best suited to lineup as the Game 2 starter.
As I mentioned previously, the Dodgers did elect to start Snell in Game 1 of the National League Wild Card Series last year, but I do think there will be a change of guard this year.
The Dodgers didn’t go and acquire Skubal to be their Game 3 starter; they acquired him to be their bonafide ace and lead them to another World Series title. It only fits best that he takes the ball for Game 1, meaning Snell would line up best for Game 3.
Skubal, being a two-time Cy Young award winner, two-time All-Star, Triple Crown winner and two-time ERA title winner, indicates that he is more than ready and able to be the Dodgers rotation anchor and leader when October baseball rolls around in a few weeks.
